literal:
The Historical Flood Narrative

Genesis 7 presents the climactic moment of Noah's obedience to God's command. The Lord instructs Noah to enter the ark with his household, specifying "of all clean beasts take seven and seven, the male and the female; but of the beasts that are unclean two and two, the male and the female" (Gen 7:2). This distinction between clean and unclean animals, appearing here before the Mosaic Law, indicates that God had communicated the knowledge of sacrifice to mankind from earliest times, as evidenced by the acceptable sacrifice of Abel in Genesis 4.

The text provides precise chronological details: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came upon the earth (Gen 7:6). St. Jerome clarifies an important point regarding the 120 years mentioned earlier in Genesis 6:3: "Human life is not reduced to 120 years, as many erroneously presumed, but 120 years was given for repentance to that generation." This interpretation is confirmed by the fact that Abraham later lived 175 years, and others lived more than 200 or 300 years after the flood.

The flood's onset is described with dual imagery: "All the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and the floodgates of heaven were opened" (Gen 7:11). Didymus the Blind explains that "the fountains of the deep were spilled and provided the source," and notes that "there is nothing improbable in God's increasing the quantity of the water, just as in the Gospels he had increased the number from five to five thousand." The rain continued for forty days and forty nights, and the waters prevailed upon the earth for one hundred and fifty days.

St. John Chrysostom observed that one hundred years passed between God's warning and the flood, and in these years the people "did not even improve the smallest bit," although they were taught to do so by Noah's building of the ark. Chrysostom emphasizes God's mercy in extending the destruction over forty days: if God had wished, he "could, at a moment, inundate everything," but "listening to his clemency, he employed many days" to give people opportunity to repent.

The closing of the ark bears particular significance. Genesis 7:16 states that "the Lord shut him in." Chrysostom sees this as an example of God's tender care: "Notice in this place too the considerateness in the expression... to teach us that he had ensured the good man's complete safety."

Tertullian, writing in the second century, noted physical evidence of the flood's universality: "Marine conchs and tritons' horns sojourn as foreigners on the mountains, eager to prove to Plato that even the heights have undulated." The Church Fathers, including Justin Martyr, Theophilus of Antioch, Gregory of Nazianzus, John Chrysostom, and Augustine of Hippo, firmly maintained the global extent of the deluge based on the testimony of the biblical text.
allegorical:
The Ark as Type of the Church

Since the time of the Church Fathers, the ark has been understood as a type of the Church. St. Peter himself establishes this connection in his first epistle: "Wherein few, that is, eight souls, were saved by water. Whereunto baptism, being of the like form, now saveth you also" (1 Pet 3:20-21). Just as the ark was the means by which Noah and his family were spared destruction, so also the Church is the instrument by which Christians are saved.

St. Augustine was the most ingenious interpreter of this typology, discussing at length how every detail of the ark's construction symbolizes some aspect of the Church. In his Contra Faustum, Augustine argues that "the ark represents the primary means of salvation in the New Testament—the wood of the cross and the waters of baptism by which original sin is washed away."

Augustine finds profound meaning in each element:

  • The door in the ark's side symbolizes the lance wound in Christ's side, through which the sacraments of baptism and the Eucharist flowed (water and blood), and through which believers enter the Church.
  • The pitch that sealed the ark symbolizes love, which holds the Church together: "For pitch is a glutinous substance, of great energy and force, to represent the ardor of love which, with great power of endurance, bears all things in the maintenance of spiritual communion."
  • The squared timbers signify "the immoveable steadiness of the life of the saints; for however you turn a cube, it still stands."
  • The ark's dimensions represent Christ's body: "For the length of the human body, from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot, is six times its breadth from side to side, and ten times its depth or thickness."
  • The ark finished in a cubit above signifies "the Church, the body of Christ gathered into unity, is raised to perfection."

The Waters of Baptism

St. Ambrose, in his treatise On the Mysteries, explains how the flood prefigures baptism:

  • "The water is that in which the flesh is dipped, that all carnal sin may be washed away. All wickedness is there buried."
  • "The wood is that on which the Lord Jesus was fastened when He suffered for us."
  • "The dove is that in the form of which the Holy Spirit descended, Who inspires peace of soul and tranquility of mind."

The deluge which washed away all the ungodly is analogous to the rite of baptism which symbolically washes away sin from the believer. As St. Cyril of Jerusalem teaches in his Catechetical Lectures: "Where a covenant is made with any, there is water also. After the flood, a covenant was made with Noah."

The Clean Animals and the Eucharist

The distinction between clean and unclean animals carries sacrificial significance. The clean animals, taken in sevens, were destined for sacrifice to God (Gen 8:20). These prefigure the pure and unblemished sacrifice of Christ in the Eucharist. As Noah preserved the clean animals for offering to God upon emerging from the ark, so the Church preserves the eucharistic sacrifice as the perpetual offering of the New Covenant.

The Hundred Years of Construction

Augustine interprets the hundred years of ark construction allegorically, noting that it "shows that the ark was made during one hundred years, which seem to correspond to the years of an age of the world. So the sixth age is occupied with the construction of the Church by the preaching of the gospel."
moral:
The Virtue of Obedience and the Urgency of Repentance

Noah stands as the supreme exemplar of faithful obedience in the face of an apparently absurd command. St. Ambrose writes: "Many appear to men to be just; few appear so to God. They appear one way to men, another way to God. To men, according to the appearance of their life; to God, according to the purity of their soul, the truth of their virtue. Men examine external things; God considers those that are within."

Noah's obedience was complete and immediate. The sacred text repeatedly emphasizes: "And Noe did all things which God commanded him" (Gen 6:22; 7:5). This perfect conformity to the divine will, even when the command seemed unreasonable by human standards, demonstrates the essence of biblical faith. Noah built an ark on dry land, far from any sea, preparing for a catastrophe that human experience had never witnessed.

The Hardness of Heart

St. John Chrysostom draws a sobering lesson from the impenitence of Noah's generation: "Noah, a man who had reached the highest peak of virtue, constructing the ark with such zeal should have been enough to instill distress and persuade people to repent before such a gentle and merciful Lord." Yet they refused.

St. Ephrem the Syrian marvels at this hardness: when the people of that generation gathered to see Noah building the ark, "it was not to repent, but rather to amuse themselves." Even when the animals miraculously assembled and entered the ark in peace—"no lion remembered its jungle and no species of beast or bird visited its customary haunt"—the people "were still not persuaded to renounce their evil deeds."

Pseudo-Basil of Caesarea notes that even in the final seven days before the flood, when Noah made one last attempt to warn them, "they did not do so at all. But I think that if they have showed repentance in those seven days, the wrath would not have come upon them."

The Urgency of Response

The moral lesson is clear: there is an appointed time for repentance, and those who delay may find the door of salvation closed. When "the Lord shut him in" (Gen 7:16), the time for entering the ark had passed. No amount of pounding on the door or crying for mercy could reopen what God had sealed.

Our Lord Himself draws this parallel in His teaching on the end times: "For as in the days before the flood, they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, even till that day in which Noe entered into the ark, and they knew not till the flood came, and took them all away" (Matt 24:38-39). The point is not that these activities were sinful in themselves, but that preoccupation with worldly concerns blinded them to the urgency of their spiritual state.

Didymus on Continence

Didymus the Blind notes a detail regarding the arrangement within the ark: Noah's family entered with couples separated—men apart from women. He explains that "it was not fitting for them to enjoy marital intercourse when such punishment was befalling everyone." This teaches the appropriateness of mortification and abstinence in times of divine judgment and the need for solidarity with those who suffer.

The Fate of the Disobedient

The universal destruction of all flesh outside the ark stands as a permanent testimony to the consequences of persistent rebellion against God. Chrysostom explains that God willed that "at least some might escape when they would see their creatures perish." God's patience extended even through the forty days of the flood itself, giving opportunity for interior repentance even as the waters rose. Yet Scripture records no conversion.
anagogical:
The Flood as Type of the Final Judgment

The flood narrative points forward to the eschatological judgment at the end of time. St. Peter makes this connection explicit: "The world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished: But the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men" (2 Pet 3:5-7). As the ancient world perished by water, so the present world awaits judgment by fire.

Our Lord establishes the definitive typological link between Noah's day and His second coming: "As it was in the days of Noe, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" (Matt 24:37). The comparison emphasizes the suddenness and unexpectedness of divine judgment upon a world absorbed in temporal concerns, oblivious to eternal realities.

The Remnant Saved Through the Ark

Only eight souls were saved through the flood—Noah, his wife, his three sons, and their wives. This small remnant, preserved through the waters of destruction, prefigures the elect who will be saved through the Church at the final judgment. As St. Gregory of Nazianzus described Noah, he was "entrusted with the saving of the whole world from the waters" and escaped destruction "in a small ark."

The pattern of divine judgment throughout Scripture confirms this: God's wrath targets the unjust while the just are spared. As with Noah, so with Lot at Sodom—the righteous are delivered while the wicked perish. This will be fulfilled definitively at the last judgment, when the Son of Man will separate the sheep from the goats (Matt 25:31-46).

The Irremediable Separation

When the Lord shut Noah in the ark, He simultaneously shut out all others. This closing of the door typifies the finality of the last judgment. As our Lord taught in the parable of the wise and foolish virgins, when the bridegroom comes and those who are ready enter with him, "the door was shut" (Matt 25:10). Those who came later crying "Lord, Lord, open to us" received the terrible response: "Amen I say to you, I know you not."

The Church Fathers understood Matthew 24:40-41—"Then two shall be in the field: one shall be taken, and one shall be left"—in light of the flood narrative. Just as those unprepared in Noah's day were "taken away" by the flood in judgment, so at Christ's return there will be an irremediable separation between the just and unjust, believers and unbelievers.

The New World Emerging from the Waters

After the flood, Noah emerged onto a cleansed earth to begin anew. This prefigures the new heavens and new earth that will emerge after the final judgment. As the flood washed away the corruption of the old world, so the final conflagration will purify creation, preparing for the eternal kingdom where "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and death shall be no more" (Apoc 21:4).

The rainbow given to Noah as a sign of God's covenant that He would never again destroy the earth by water points beyond itself to the definitive covenant in Christ's blood, which promises not merely preservation from temporal destruction but eternal life in the world to come. The ark that carried Noah through the waters of judgment to a renewed earth is thus a figure of the Church, which carries the faithful through the present age of trial to the eternal Jerusalem.

Vigilance and Preparation

The anagogical sense calls the faithful to constant vigilance. As the Church Fathers noted, the people of Noah's day were not engaged in particularly heinous sins when judgment came—they were simply living ordinary lives, eating, drinking, marrying. Their fault was not awareness of coming judgment but indifference to it. The same danger threatens every generation. The flood stands as perpetual warning that "of that day and hour no one knoweth" (Matt 24:36), and therefore the wise will be always prepared, having entered the ark of the Church and remained faithful within her saving walls.
